feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The paperwork that stands between an older adult and paid-for care keeps getting harder to argue with, and the federally funded help on the other side of it is being topped up in five-figure increments. An Administration for Community Living notice published 09/10/26 announces a single-source administrative supplement of $226,000 to the Senior Medicare Patrol Resource Center cooperative agreement held by the Northeast Iowa Area Agency on Aging, bringing the FY 2026 total to $1,226,000. On the same day, KFF published two pieces from the other side of the counter: one finding prior authorization is the single biggest burden insured adults report beyond cost, the other breaking down how much of every premium dollar goes to insurer administrative costs and profit and how that share varies across private insurance markets and Medicare. Together they describe a system where the decision to cover something is contested paperwork, and the only named national infrastructure for helping a beneficiary contest it runs on a little over a million dollars a year.

**Why it matters:** The stake is help, not coverage. A beneficiary who suspects an error on a Medicare statement, or who is told a service needs authorization first, is looking for someone to walk it through with them, and the record now names what that support is funded at: $1,226,000 for the national resource center behind the Senior Medicare Patrol network in FY 2026, $226,000 of it added mid-year. The ACL notice does not say how many beneficiaries that reaches, and this piece should not pretend otherwise. What it can say is that prior authorization was named the biggest burden after price in KFF polling, that the share of premium dollars going to overhead and profit is now published and varies by market, and that the counterweight is one cooperative agreement with a dollar figure attached to it.

**Why pitch this now:** The ACL notice is dated 09/10/26 and the award is for FY 2026, so the money and the fiscal year are both live. Both KFF pieces published 09/10/26. And the cost backdrop moved: BLS medical care CPI printed 593.00 in August 2026, up 1.6% year over year, against 593.78 and +1.7% for July 2026, so prices are still climbing but the pace eased between the two prints.

**Angle:** Whether the help an older adult can actually reach when a bill or an authorization looks wrong is sized anything like the paperwork it exists to answer. Working title: "Who answers when the Medicare statement is wrong." For family caregivers and beneficiaries handling somebody else's coverage, with a second read for the agencies-on-aging network that delivers this counseling.

**Potential headlines:**
- A $226,000 supplement decides how much help you get reading a Medicare bill
- Prior authorization is the biggest hassle after the price, and one federal program answers the phone
- Where your premium dollar goes before it pays for any care

**Potential outlets:**
- **Next Avenue** — its readers are the adult children already on the phone about a parent's statement, and this is a service story with a federal document under it.
- **Bankrate Retirement** — treats Medicare as a household finance problem, which is exactly what a disputed bill and a 1.6% medical care CPI are.
- **USA Today** — the Senior Medicare Patrol network is delivered locally, so the Gannett papers can name the agency that does it in their state.
- **LeadingAge** — its provider and area-agency members are the delivery end of ACL cooperative agreements and will read a mid-year supplement as a capacity question.

**The federal program that helps you challenge a Medicare bill runs on $1.2 million**
*Announcing the Intent To Award a Single-Source Supplement to the Senior Medicare Patrol (SMP) Resource Center*  
- Angle: A plain read of the 09/10/26 ACL notice — a $226,000 supplement, $1,226,000 total for FY 2026 — for beneficiaries and the adult children who handle their statements.
- Hook: A mid-year single-source supplement puts a dollar figure on the national infrastructure behind Senior Medicare Patrol counseling.
- For readers: If a charge on your Medicare summary notice looks wrong, find your state's Senior Medicare Patrol before you call the provider, and keep the statement with the dates and the service codes on it.
- For the trade: Area agencies on aging and their partners should read a mid-year administrative supplement as a signal about resource-center support capacity for the rest of FY 2026.
- Why it matters: Knowing the program exists is the difference between eating a questionable charge and getting someone to work it with you.
- Also: Localizable: the notice names the Northeast Iowa Area Agency on Aging as the resource center grantee, and every state has its own SMP to name locally. No monitored publisher matched it.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**Medical prices are still rising, just a little slower than last month's print**
*BLS: Consumer Price Index, medical care, August 2026 — 593 index 1982-84=100 (+1.6% year over year)*  
- Angle: A short chart piece setting August 2026's 593.00 and +1.6% against the July 2026 print of 593.78 and +1.7%, for retirees building next year's health budget.
- Hook: The medical care index moved between prints, and the year-over-year pace eased from 1.7% to 1.6%.
- For readers: Use the 1.6% figure as the floor when you estimate next year's out-of-pocket health spending, not the general inflation number you see in headlines.
- For the trade: For operators and benefit designers, a decelerating medical care index changes the assumption baked into next year's rate and premium conversations.
- Why it matters: Budgeting a fixed income against the wrong inflation figure is how a health year goes over.
- Also: Chartable monthly series; no monitored publisher matched this print.
- Pitch to: Bankrate Retirement, Forbes Retirement

**How much of your premium dollar never becomes care**
*What Do We Get for the Cut Health Insurers Take?*  
- Angle: An explainer built on KFF's 09/10/26 breakdown of administrative costs and profit and how that share varies across private insurance markets and Medicare, for people choosing a plan.
- Hook: KFF published the overhead-and-profit share by market on 09/10/26, and no monitored publisher matched it.
- For readers: When you compare plans this fall, ask what the plan spends on care versus administration, not just what the premium is.
- For the trade: Payers and the providers who contract with them get a published benchmark for the administrative share argument that usually happens without numbers.
- Why it matters: The share of your premium that goes to overhead is money you are paying and not receiving care for.
- Also: National, not localizable; confirmed gap among monitored publishers.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**Beyond the price, prior authorization is the thing insured adults hate most**
*Who Do We Trust to Decide What Health Care Gets Covered, and at What Price?*  
- Angle: A reader piece on the KFF poll finding prior authorization is the single biggest burden insured adults report beyond cost, aimed at people about to be told a service needs approval first.
- Hook: KFF's 09/10/26 poll names prior authorization the top burden after cost, in a system where coverage decisions sit with insurers.
- For readers: Ask your plan in writing whether a service needs prior authorization before it is scheduled, and get the decision and its date in the same form.
- For the trade: Providers can point to polled patient burden, not just their own administrative cost, when they argue authorization volume with plans.
- Why it matters: An unapproved service can turn into a bill you owe in full.
- Also: Confirmed gap; distinct from the insurer-metrics analysis this brief used on 09/09/26, since this is polling on burden rather than denial rates.
- Pitch to: National Council on Aging

**Home care added jobs more than twice as fast as nursing homes this year**
*BLS: Home health care services employment, August 2026 — 1,896.40 thousands of jobs (+5.0% year over year)*  
- Angle: A single comparison — home health at 1,896.40 thousand jobs and +5.0% against nursing care facilities at 1,590.20 thousand and +2.1% — for families deciding whether care comes to the house or the other way around.
- Hook: The two care settings' employment lines are moving at very different speeds in the same August print.
- For readers: If you are weighing home care against a facility, the hiring numbers say aides are being added faster in home-based services, which is where you are likelier to find availability.
- For the trade: Skilled nursing operators are competing for the same aides with a home care sector growing at 5.0%, which sets the floor for what a recruitment plan has to beat.
- Why it matters: Which sector is hiring decides how long you wait for a caregiver and how often the one you get changes.
- Also: Monthly, chartable, localizable by state; confirmed gap on both series.
- Pitch to: Next Avenue, Caring.com

**Nursing homes are still staffing back up at 2 percent a year**
*BLS: Nursing care facilities employment, August 2026 — 1,590.20 thousands of jobs (+2.1% year over year)*  
- Angle: A staffing-recovery read on the 1,590.20 thousand August figure for readers comparing facilities and for the operators hiring into them.
- Hook: A +2.1% annual gain is real growth and also a slow one, against a home care sector at +5.0%.
- For readers: When you tour a nursing home, ask how many open aide and nurse positions it has right now and how it covers an uncovered shift.
- For the trade: Slow sector-wide headcount growth is the context for every staffing-standard and agency-cost conversation an operator is having this quarter.
- Why it matters: Staffing level is the single thing most closely tied to the care your relative actually receives each shift.
- Also: Confirmed gap; pairs directly with the home health series for a two-line chart.
- Pitch to: Provider Magazine, McKnight's Home Care

**The people caring for your parent earn $25.65 an hour in assisted living, $28.04 in home care**
*BLS: Assisted living and CCRC average hourly earnings, July 2026 — 25.65 dollars per hour (+3.2% year over year)*  
- Angle: A pay-comparison piece setting assisted living and CCRC earnings of $25.65 and +3.2% against home health services at $28.04 and +2.0%, for families who wonder why staff keep changing.
- Hook: Assisted living pay is rising faster in percentage terms while still sitting below home health in dollars.
- For readers: Ask a community what it pays its aides and what its turnover was last year; the answer predicts whether the person who knows your parent will still be there in six months.
- For the trade: Senior living operators are raising wages faster than home health and still trailing on the hourly number, which is the recruiting problem stated as arithmetic.
- Why it matters: Staff turnover is the quality problem families feel first, and pay is the part of it you can ask about.
- Also: Two BLS wage series that have gone unused in this brief's recent pitches; both confirmed gaps.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Senior Living, SeniorLiving.org

**The rent your voucher will cover changes on October 1**
*Fair Market Rents for the Housing Choice Voucher Program, Moderate Rehabilitation Single Room Occupancy Program, and Other Programs, Fiscal Year 2027*  
- Angle: A walkthrough of HUD's FY 2027 Fair Market Rents notice, published 09/01/26, including the reevaluation process open to public housing agencies, for older renters on vouchers.
- Hook: FMRs are adjusted to take effect October 1 each year, and the FY 2027 methodology and reevaluation procedures are now published.
- For readers: Check your metro's new FMR before you renew, and ask your housing agency whether it is requesting a reevaluation if the published figure looks below local asking rents.
- For the trade: Affordable senior housing owners and developers underwrite against these numbers, and the reevaluation window is the only lever on a figure that sets revenue for the year.
- Why it matters: An FMR set below what landlords actually charge is the difference between a voucher that works and one nobody will take.
- Also: Localizable to every metro; confirmed gap, with a hard October 1 effective date.
- Pitch to: Senior Housing News, Next Avenue

**Find out which chain your nursing home belongs to**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Facility Affiliation Data*  
- Angle: A how-to on using the refreshed facility affiliation file to see what else a provider is connected to, for families comparing two homes in the same county.
- Hook: The publicly reported affiliation file was refreshed 08/18/26, letting a family follow a facility to its wider group.
- For readers: Look up your shortlisted homes' affiliations, then check the survey and penalty records of the other facilities in the same group before you sign anything.
- For the trade: Affiliation-level comparisons are how reporters and referral sources will increasingly judge a group rather than a single building.
- Why it matters: A problem that shows up across a chain tells you more than one good inspection at one address.
- Also: Refreshed file rather than an event; state and county level, so localizable. Lightly covered among monitored publishers.
- Pitch to: Skilled Nursing News, Family Caregiver Alliance

**What patients said about your doctor's practice, not just your doctor**
*CMS refreshed dataset: PY 2024 Group Public Reporting: Patient Experience*  
- Angle: A short piece on the refreshed PY 2024 group-level CAHPS for MIPS file, for patients who want to judge the practice they actually call.
- Hook: Patient experience results submitted by groups were refreshed 08/18/26 at the group rather than individual clinician level.
- For readers: If you are switching practices, look at the group's patient experience results alongside the clinician you were referred to.
- For the trade: Group-level reporting means a practice's survey results follow the whole organization, which matters for medical groups affiliated with post-acute and senior care providers.
- Why it matters: The practice's front desk, scheduling and follow-up are most of your experience of care, and they are what group-level surveys capture.
- Also: Refreshed data file, not an event; state and county geographies available.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Long-Term Care News, Bankrate Retirement

**The meeting that decides which new treatments Medicare pays extra for**
*Medicare Program; Town Hall Meeting on the Fiscal Year 2028 Applications for New Technology Add-On Payments*  
- Angle: A process explainer on the 09/08/26 notice of a virtual town hall on FY 2028 new technology add-on payment applications under the inpatient prospective payment system, for readers who want to know how a new device gets paid for.
- Hook: Interested parties are invited to comment on FY 2028 applications at a virtual meeting announced under the Social Security Act's town hall requirement.
- For readers: If a new device or therapy matters to your household, this is the public meeting where the payment case for it gets argued, and comment is open to the public.
- For the trade: Hospitals, device makers and post-acute partners should read the application list as a preview of what inpatient payment will support in FY 2028.
- Why it matters: Whether Medicare pays extra for a new technology shapes which hospitals offer it and where you have to travel to get it.
- Also: Confirmed gap; fixed meeting date gives it a short news window.
- Pitch to: Fierce Healthcare, ThinkAdvisor

**A Los Angeles program for adults with mental health and substance use needs gets its results published**
*Implementation and Outcome Evaluation of LA DOOR, a Proposition 47–Funded Program in Los Angeles*  
- Angle: A read of the 09/10/26 RAND evaluation of LA DOOR Cohort 3, covering September 2022 through December 2025, for readers and providers tracking behavioral health supports for adults with justice involvement.
- Hook: A named local program's process and outcome evaluation is now on the record, published 09/10/26 and unmatched by monitored publishers.
- For readers: If you are helping an adult relative with substance use or mental health needs and a court history, this evaluation shows what one funded program actually delivered and over what period.
- For the trade: Behavioral health and home-based providers can use a published county-level evaluation as the template for what funders will ask their own programs to show.
- Why it matters: Families navigating behavioral health services rarely get to see whether a program worked before they enroll someone in it.
- Also: Los Angeles specific; depression and mental health was the fastest-rising topic this run, up two items.
- Pitch to: Generations Today, Next Avenue
